Mode Mixture: Practice for Chapter 19

Exercises for Chapter 19 of Hutchinson’s Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom: chords borrowed from the parallel minor (i, ii°, iiø7, ♭III, iv, v, ♭VI, ♭VII, ♭VII7, vii°7), naming and writing them with figures, lead-sheet symbols, the deceptive cadence to ♭VI, the Picardy third, and the book’s listening examples.

This page goes with Chapter 19, Mode Mixture of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first; the book is the reference for the terms used here. It follows Chapter 18, Secondary Diminished Chords, and uses the Roman numerals of Chapter 7 and the seventh chords of Chapter 8.

Every drill has Settings, and is also on the Theory Drills page.

Typing a borrowed chord: case and the sign after the numeral give the quality, as always: iv, ii°, iiø7, vii°7, ♭VI, ♭VII7. Type b for ♭ (bVI), o for °, h for ø. Inversions take the figures 6 and 64 for triads, 65, 43 and 42 for seventh chords: iv6, ♭VI64, iiø65, vii°42.

19.1 Mode mixture

Mode mixture means using, in a major key, chords that belong to the parallel minor (the minor key on the same tonic). The book also calls them borrowed chords. You spot them by their lowered notes: most often ♭6̂ (A♭ in C major), sometimes ♭3̂ (E♭) and ♭7̂ (B♭). Listen for the sudden darkening when a minor-key chord appears in a major-key passage. Read 19.1

19.2 Which chords contain the borrowed notes

Put a lowered note into the major key’s chords and their quality changes. The book lists each place ♭6̂, ♭3̂ and ♭7̂ can sit. In C major:

Borrowed note as root as 3rd as 5th as 7th
♭6̂ (A♭) ♭VI (A♭ C E♭) iv (F A♭ C) ii° (D F A♭), iiø7 (D F A♭ C) vii°7 (B D F A♭), ♭VII7 (B♭ D F A♭)
♭3̂ (E♭) ♭III (E♭ G B♭) i (C E♭ G) ♭VI (A♭ C E♭)
♭7̂ (B♭) ♭VII (B♭ D F) v (G B♭ D) ♭III (E♭ G B♭)

The book’s advice: you don’t need to memorize the list. What matters is seeing that a minor-key note changes the quality of the chord it sits in. The drills add iv7 (F A♭ C E♭), which is not in the book’s two figures. Read 19.2

19.3 Analysing and writing borrowed chords

Analysing a borrowed chord is easier than analysing a secondary chord: there is no slash. You give its root, quality and inversion, as for any chord. The book’s example: in G major, the notes C–E♭–G–A stack in thirds as A–C–E♭–G. The root is A (2̂), the thirds are m3–m3–M3, so it is half-diminished, and C (the 3rd) is in the bass: iiø65.

To write one, read the numeral’s quality carefully. The ♭ in ♭VI means the root is a half step below the major key’s 6̂; it does not mean “write a flat”. In A major, 6̂ is F♯, so ♭VI is built on F♮: F–A–C. Read 19.3

19.4 The deceptive cadence with ♭VI

The usual deceptive cadence goes V–vi. Going instead to the major chord on ♭6̂, V–♭VI, is a stronger surprise. The book’s examples are endings of “The Star-Spangled Banner” as sung at Super Bowls and inaugurations, where ♭VI then moves to ♭VII and I. Read 19.4

Listen: the book’s examples

By ear: the phrase is I, then IV or ii, then V, then either vi or ♭VI. Which one? (The staff appears after you answer.)

19.5 The Picardy third

Borrowing the other way, from major into minor, is rare. The one common case is the last chord of a minor-key piece: a major I instead of i. Its raised 3rd is the Picardy third. The book notes it was most common in the Baroque, and is still used now and then. Read 19.5

A minor-key phrase, i, then iv or VI, then V, then the tonic. Does it end minor or major?

For teachers
  • Links with your settings: open a drill’s Settings, then Copy a link with these settings. Add &lock=1 for a test, &count=20 for a score.
  • Chords drilled: the book’s Figures 19.2.1 and 19.2.2: i, ii°, iiø7, ♭III, iv, v, ♭VI, ♭VII, ♭VII7 and vii°7, in major keys, plus iv7, which is not in those figures. Pick any of them under Settings → Chords. Every one has at least one note outside the key signature, and no two of them, nor any diatonic chord of the major key, have the same spelled notes, so each question has one answer. Keys that would need a double flat for a chord are skipped for that chord.
  • Numerals: as in the book: no slash, case and ° / ø for quality, ♭ before the numeral for a lowered root. vii°7 has no ♭, as in the book’s figure and its exercise 1 (D: vii°42).
  • Ear drills: four chords, one a bar, root in the bass and a close triad above. The deceptive cadence drill is I, IV or ii, V, then vi or ♭VI; the Picardy drill is i, iv or VI, V, then i or I.
  • Voicing: close position above the bass. The drills are for spelling and labelling, not for voice leading.
  • Checked: node tests/lessons/mixture-drill.test.js generates about 14,000 questions and checks each against its own table of the chords in C moved to the question’s key: the spelling, the figure, a chromatic note, one answer only, the drawn ABC sounding the same notes, and the typed forms the page promises.
  • Videos: the clips use the book’s YouTube links and start and end times; each was checked against YouTube. Some are covers or other recordings rather than the writers’ own: “Blackbird” is Sarah McLachlan’s recording, “Beautiful” is Christina Aguilera’s, “Joy to the World” is Three Dog Night’s, and “One Day I’ll Fly Away” is a lyrics video of the Moulin Rouge! version on a fan channel.
